chapter: Ben Webster and Jim and Andy's
title: Hurley's, Charlie's and the absence of Black musicians
summary: Maxwell disliked Hurley's; Black musicians seldom appeared at Hurley's because NBC had none, while Hinton mentions PeeWee Russell and Tricky Sam.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Yeah, it was. They used to speak that way about Charlie's Tavern but I never went over there very much, not out of any other reason than the fact that most of my work was -- I drank at Hurley's Bar in those days, when I was at NBC. That was quite a place, too, you know. But it always gave me an uneasy feeling. I didn't like it. The people in there were -- I don't know, I just didn't like it. There was too many wrong people in there, including the governors.

From my standpoint in this same business, as I mentioned before, it was quite sometime before black musicians began to get in the studios. Well, of course, if you weren't in the studios, you didn't go in these bars.
I was just thinking about that. I was trying to remember if I ever saw black musicians in there, and I don't recall any.
Seldom did you see a black musician in Hurley's, because they didn't work at NBC. And Jim and Andy's, ABC, had the guys in there. And there weren't very many black
sitting by the window and he'd signal me in, and that would be the end of that day.

Well, I began to get a little busy, making a 10:00 o'clock date, but I kept my bass upstairs at Beefsteak before I graduated to Jim and Andy's. And I would see PeeWee Russell sitting there. In the early days, in the '30s, I used to drink in there and Joe Nanton--- Tricky Sam with Ellington 's band, he was always down at the end of the bar. He was a loner. It was a wierd place.
Yeah, well, Don Coles took his place down at the end of the bar.
Yeah, also a trombone player. I always used to see him there, too.
